A.explanation: There is no net vertical force to accelerate the molecule, so the vertical velocity cannot increase from zero.

B.explanation: Equal and opposite forces $F = qE$ on the two charges give zero resultant force, so both velocity components are unchanged.

C.explanation: There is no resultant force in either direction, so neither the horizontal nor the vertical component can increase.

D.explanation: There is no horizontal electric force, so the constant horizontal velocity from before entering the field is unchanged.

hints: Notice the molecule is a dipole with equal $+q$ and $-q$ charges that enter the vertical field lines at the same time.
Recall $F = qE$ acts parallel to the field on the positive charge and antiparallel on the negative charge, with equal magnitude.
Add the two vertical electric forces as vectors to find the resultant force and then use $F = ma$ for the centre of mass motion.
walkthrough: Identify the setup: a neutral dipole moving horizontally enters a uniform vertical downward electric field, with both charges inside the field together.
State the force rule: electric force is $F = qE$, in the direction of $E$ for the positive charge and opposite to $E$ for the negative charge.
Compare the two forces: magnitudes are equal because charge magnitudes are equal and $E$ is uniform, but directions are opposite, one down and one up.
Find the resultant: vector sum of the two forces is zero, so there is no net force and no acceleration of the molecule as a whole, although it may experience a turning effect.
Conclude the motion: with zero horizontal force the horizontal velocity stays constant, and with zero net vertical force the vertical velocity stays at zero. This is option B.
